questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1968 housing law changed what a landlord could lawfully do.
questions.stem: The intake form mentions a patient whose landlord refused to renew a lease. Explain how the Fair Housing Act of 1968 changed what a landlord could lawfully do.

answer.exemplar: The Fair Housing Act of 1968, enacted as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, made it unlawful to discriminate in the sale, rental or financing of housing on the basis of race, colour, religion or national origin. It applied to landlords, agents and sellers, and to the financing of purchases through federally related institutions. It also reached practices such as steering buyers toward certain neighbourhoods and blockbusting by using panic sales to empty an area. The law created a federal agency and a private right of action, giving tenants a way to seek relief in court.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student can state the scope of the 1968 housing law and its enforcement mechanisms. Answers that cover only selling or only race miss the reach of the statute.
questions.hint: Consider both the housing market and the agencies that financed it.

That the courts lost control of the case because officials set their own construction schedule

options.misconception: Believes only construction could satisfy the requirement

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why registration was the decisive step in the fight for southern voting rights.
questions.stem: Second opinion requested by the ward sister concerns a patient's father. Explain why registration was the decisive step in the fight for southern voting rights.

answer.exemplar: In many southern counties the legal right to vote existed on paper while the administration of registration kept eligible Black citizens off the rolls through arbitrary rules, delays and intimidation at the registrar's desk. Because the vote was counted at the polls and recorded only by voters who had appeared on the list, every person absent from that list was simply absent from the outcome. Reform that reached the registration desk therefore mattered more than any statute about the ballot itself, since registration decided who would ever reach it.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student understands registration as the practical gate to participation. Answers that treat the right to vote as sufficient miss the administrative barrier.
questions.hint: Think about what happens before a ballot is cast.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the absence of a segregation statute shaped the proof required.
questions.stem: Case conference today examined the problem of schools divided without any ordinance. Explain how the requirement of intent shaped claims against communities that had no segregation statute.

answer.exemplar: Where a state or local law had authorised segregated schools, the presence of the law itself made discriminatory purpose clear, so a plaintiff did not have to prove intent separately. Where no law authorised separation, the presumption of intent disappeared, and the plaintiff had to prove from the conduct of the local school authorities that they deliberately maintained segregation. That placed a heavier evidentiary burden on the complainants, lengthened the litigation and made outcomes turn on the particular facts of each district rather than on the existence of a rule.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student understands that the intent requirement was conditional on the presence or absence of state action. Answers that treat the rule as uniform across cases miss the distinction.
questions.hint: Consider what happened when no law authorised separation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why proof of an interdistrict violation was required before relief could cross lines.
questions.stem: Consultation request from a rural clinic describes a plan for busing that would cross district lines. Explain why a court had to find a violation crossing district lines before it could order relief across those lines.

answer.exemplar: A remedy may reach as far as the wrong it answers. If the only violation proved was within a single school district, then an order sending pupils from that district into neighbouring districts would disturb local communities that had committed no constitutional wrong and would reach into school districts that had not consented to the loss of their own property and authority. Because the reach of the remedy had to match the reach of the violation, courts required proof that segregation itself had crossed district lines, and they would not consolidate separate districts to make a broader remedy possible.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student explains the matching principle that limited interdistrict remedies. Answers that treat consolidation as automatic or as a question of convenience miss the reasoning.
questions.hint: Consider the link between the remedy's reach and the violation's reach.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1968 housing law extended rather than began the civil rights gains.
questions.stem: The medical record quotes a schoolteacher who served on a housing committee. Explain why the 1968 housing law is treated as an extension of the civil rights gains of the previous decade rather than a new departure.

answer.exemplar: By 1968 the civil rights movement had already used litigation and protest against segregation in schools and public facilities, and many white suburbs had responded by moving from explicit racial exclusion to subtler practices such as restrictive covenants, racial steering and blockbusting. The Fair Housing Act addressed exactly that newer form of discrimination, extending the principle of equal treatment into the private housing market where most Americans lived and where earlier law had done little. It also created a federal enforcement agency and a private right of action, so the law supplied remedies rather than principles alone.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student can connect the 1968 statute to the shifting tactics of discrimination and to the legal framework built in the previous decade. Answers that treat it as a complete solution miss its limits.
questions.hint: Think about how discrimination in housing had changed by the 1960s.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how examiners' arrival changed the political power of southern counties.
questions.stem: Visiting hours ended and the family asked about the county lines. Explain how examiners' arrival at the registration desk changed the political power of southern counties.

answer.exemplar: In a number of southern counties the Democratic organisation had relied on keeping Black citizens off the registration rolls to preserve one-party control, and the local courthouse was a centre of that power. When federal examiners began registering voters under uniform rules and supervising the ballot, the courthouse could no longer control who qualified, and the vote of those newly registered shifted the outcome of elections that had been settled for decades. The changes were uneven, but they turned county registration into a national issue and weakened the local organisation that had profited from exclusion.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how local arrangements without a statute were treated and what plaintiffs had to show.
questions.stem: The patient's story included the detail that her school had no law requiring segregation but had separate lines at the door. Explain how the Court treated such local arrangements and what it required of the plaintiffs who challenged them.

answer.exemplar: Where no state statute or local ordinance authorised segregated schools, the Court did not treat the separation as self-proving. Instead, a plaintiff had to show that the local school authorities had deliberately created or maintained the separation, and that showing meant evidence about board decisions, the assignment of pupils and the reasons officials gave for the patterns they produced. That made such cases slower and more fact-bound than cases in which a segregation statute existed, since the statute itself supplied the proof of purpose, and the Court stopped short of holding that every unequal school system was unconstitutional without more.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student can distinguish the treatment of officially imposed segregation from informal local separation and state the resulting burden on plaintiffs. Answers that flatten the distinction miss the framework.
questions.hint: Consider what proof the absence of a statute removed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in registration totals as evidence about the barrier to voting.
questions.stem: The social history noted a childhood spent in a school that had been closed by officials. Suppose 12,000 Black citizens of voting age lived in a county in 1960, of whom 4,500 were registered; after examiners worked the parish for two seasons, 9,000 were registered. What does the comparison show?

options.text: That registration rose from about three in eight to three in four, so the obstacle was administrative practice
That registration barely changed, so examiners had limited effect after two seasons of work
options.misconception: Believes the change between the two dates was small

options.text: That examiners lowered the voting age, which raised registration among younger citizens
options.misconception: Believes examiners lowered the voting age

options.text: That registration fell between the two dates, because examiners discouraged applications
options.misconception: Believes registration fell after examiners arrived

questions.explanation: Registration rose from 4,500 of 12,000 to 9,000 of 12,000, that is from about three in eight to three in four, which points to administrative practice rather than a legal barrier. The distractors misread the direction or invent an age change.
questions.hint: Compare each figure with the eligible total.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the enforcement provisions differed from earlier federal civil rights law.
questions.stem: During a long wait in the clinic the patient raised the subject of an agent who refused to show a flat. Explain how the enforcement provisions of the 1968 housing law differed from those of earlier federal civil rights legislation.

answer.exemplar: Earlier federal civil rights statutes had been enforced mainly through administrative complaint, so a person turned away by a landlord had to persuade a government agency to act and then wait for an investigation. The 1968 housing law created a federal agency to supervise compliance and, more importantly, gave individuals a private right of action, so a person denied housing could go to court and obtain an order and damages without first convincing an agency to act. That shift towards individual enforcement is what made the statute usable in everyday disputes over a single apartment.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student understands the change from administrative enforcement to a private right of action. Answers that describe enforcement only as an agency process miss the new avenue for individuals.
questions.hint: Think about what a tenant could do without waiting for an agency.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a phased plan that made desegregation depend on future construction.

stimulus.body: Plan submitted to the court: Phase one, construction of the four new schools, to be completed during the 1964 and 1965 school years. Phase two, assignment of pupils to integrated schools, to commence in the school year following the completion of phase one and the opening of the term.

questions.stem: Chart entries from a county clinic describe a family that had waited through those years. What does the plan reveal about the treatment of delay?

options.text: That the plan tied the end of segregation to a future building timetable rather than to an immediate duty
That the district had already desegregated and was merely adding new buildings for comfort
options.misconception: Believes desegregation was already complete when the plan was filed

options.text: That the court had approved the plan and so had ended the litigation over segregation
options.misconception: Believes the court had already approved the plan

options.text: That the delay was necessary because the new buildings had to be ready before pupils could be transferred
options.misconception: Believes construction had to finish before any transfer could occur

questions.explanation: A plan that makes pupil assignment conditional on future construction puts the end of segregation in the hands of a building schedule, which is the practice the Court criticised as delay. The distractors misread the plan's stage, its status and the necessity it claimed.
questions.hint: Notice what the plan made the next step depend on.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the limits the Court placed on remedies crossing district lines.
questions.stem: The patient's grandson asked whether the law still protects families today. Which combination best describes the limits the Court placed on remedies crossing district lines?

options.text: Remedies stayed within districts unless an interdistrict violation was proved, and districts were not merged to widen relief
Remedies could always cross district lines, but only after a referendum of the affected communities
options.misconception: Believes interdistrict remedies required a local referendum

options.text: Congress had to approve any remedy that reached beyond a single district before it took effect
options.misconception: Believes Congress had to approve interdistrict remedies

options.text: Courts could merge districts whenever a metropolitan area could be shown to be a single community
options.misconception: Believes courts could merge districts at will

questions.explanation: The limits were tied to the proof of a violation and the autonomy of separate districts, so a remedy crossing lines needed an interdistrict violation and consolidation was not a shortcut. The distractors invent referendums, congressional approval and free consolidation.
questions.hint: Consider what had to be proved before a remedy could cross lines.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A housing remedy beyond the city
questions.learningObjective: Identify the principle that permitted suburban placements in housing remedies.
questions.stem: Discharge instructions mentioned checking voter registration because the family had moved. Which principle allowed a court to consider placing families in suburban housing units?

options.text: That a remedy for the agency's discrimination could reach the whole metropolitan area it served
That suburbs were legally part of the city for housing purposes after 1968
options.misconception: Believes suburbs were legally absorbed into the city

options.text: That the federal government could condemn suburban housing for public use
options.misconception: Believes the government could condemn suburban housing

options.text: That local zoning decisions were void whenever they produced unequal outcomes
options.misconception: Believes all zoning decisions with unequal outcomes were void

questions.explanation: Because the wrongdoing lay with an agency serving a metropolitan area, the court could consider a remedy reaching beyond the municipal boundary, and it did so without requiring suburban consent. The distractors invent legal merger, condemnation and a general rule against zoning.
questions.hint: Consider the reach of the agency that had done the wrong.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why private restrictive covenants were treated as a constitutional problem.
questions.stem: The patient explained that her family had moved because a neighbourhood refused to sell to them. How did the Supreme Court treat racially restrictive covenants that private owners had signed?

options.text: As unenforceable, because courts enforcing them acted for the state and equal protection reached that action
As valid private contracts, since they bound only the people who had signed them
options.misconception: Believes the covenants were valid private contracts

options.text: As federal crimes, punishable by fine for any person who enforced them
options.misconception: Believes enforcing a covenant was a federal crime

options.text: As valid until repealed by a state legislature, which many states never did
options.misconception: Believes the covenants stayed valid until state repeal

questions.explanation: Because enforcement of the covenant ran through the courts, and courts are organs of the state, the equal protection guarantee applied and the covenants could not be enforced. The distractors treat the covenants as valid contracts, as crimes or as dependent on state repeal.
questions.hint: Consider which institution gave the covenant its force.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Federal examiners at the registration desk
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of an electorate added through federal registration.
questions.stem: The clinic's receptionist remembered the courthouse queue. Suppose examiners served in 45 counties and registered 675,000 new voters, while the registered electorate in those counties stood at 5.4 million. What does that ratio suggest?

options.text: About one in eight, so a substantial bloc of previously excluded citizens entered the electorate at once
About one in two, so most of the electorate in those counties was newly registered
options.misconception: Believes about half the electorate was newly registered

options.text: About one in a hundred, so the examiners had a negligible effect on registration
options.misconception: Believes the examiners' effect was negligible

options.text: About three in four, so examiners registered nearly all eligible citizens
options.misconception: Believes examiners registered nearly all eligible citizens

questions.explanation: Six hundred seventy-five thousand out of 5.4 million is about one in eight, a large bloc of voters who had previously been excluded, which changed the arithmetic of close elections. The distractors misplace the proportion or dismiss the effect.
questions.hint: Divide new registrations by the registered electorate.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why uniform registration rules mattered more than careful supervision of voting.
questions.stem: A resident of the county told the nurse about her father's poll book. Explain why uniform registration rules mattered more to the outcome of elections than careful supervision of the voting itself.

answer.exemplar: Registration decided who would appear in the polling place at all, because the roll, not the ballot, was the gateway. If a registrar could turn away an applicant for a reason that varied from one applicant to the next, then no amount of care at the polling place would bring those citizens into the count. Once examiners applied the same published criteria in the same way to every applicant, the rolls began to reflect the eligible population rather than the registrar's judgement, and the number of voters who actually cast ballots rose accordingly. Supervision of the voting mattered, but it operated downstream of that earlier decision.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student understands registration as the decisive gate rather than one step among several. Answers that treat the polling place as the decisive point miss the sequence.
questions.hint: Think about the step that came before the ballot.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how the poll tax was enforced through official records.

stimulus.body: Notice to the sheriff: Payment of the poll tax of one dollar is required of every person wishing to vote at the next election. The list of persons who have paid is maintained at this office and is open to inspection, so that persons who have not paid may be identified before the election.

questions.stem: The admission notes record a form carried to the courthouse in 1960. Given the notice below, what does it show about how the poll tax was enforced?

options.text: That payment was recorded in a list officials could inspect, which made the tax usable to identify and challenge voters
That the tax was collected automatically from wages and never required a direct payment
options.misconception: Believes the tax was withheld automatically from wages

options.text: That payment could be made only at the courthouse on election day, so no list was kept
options.misconception: Believes payment was possible only on election day

options.text: That the county collected the tax but did not record who had paid, so no one could be identified
options.misconception: Believes no record of payment was kept

questions.explanation: The notice shows the tax functioning as a list-driven condition of voting, since the record of payment made non-payment visible to officials who could use it against a voter. The distractors invent automatic collection, a single payment window and no record.
questions.hint: Notice what the office kept and what it was used for.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the place of the 1968 housing law within the civil rights movement.
questions.stem: The patient's cousin wrote about the family's move in 1968. Which combination best describes the 1968 housing law as a culmination of the civil rights movement?

options.text: It extended the principle of equal treatment into the private housing market, where most Americans lived
It ended segregation in the public schools, which had been the movement's main achievement
options.misconception: Believes the law ended school segregation

options.text: It created federal examiners to supervise housing elections and register families
options.misconception: Believes the law created housing examiners

options.text: It replaced state housing codes with a single national building standard
options.misconception: Believes the law set national building standards

questions.explanation: After a decade of action against segregation in schools and public facilities, the 1968 law reached the private housing market, where most Americans lived and where earlier federal law had done little. The distractors misidentify the subject of the statute and its provisions.
questions.hint: Consider where most Americans actually lived.
